qs.q: MSTOM 42 100 kg, MSLM 35 000 kg, PLLM 33 000 kg, MZFM 31 000 kg, DOM 19 000 kg, fuel capacity 12 500 kg, max trip fuel 9000 kg, contingency 1000 kg, alternate 500 kg, final reserve 400 kg. What are the maximum take-off mass and maximum traffic load?
qs.ex: RTOM is the least of: PLLM + trip fuel = 42 000; MZFM + take-off fuel (9000 + 1000 + 500 + 400) = 41 900; MSTOM 42 100. So 41 900 kg; traffic load = 41 900 − 19 000 − 10 900 = 12 000 kg.

qs.q: The centre of gravity of an aeroplane is that point through which the total mass of the aeroplane is said to act. The weight acts in a direction
o: governed by the distribution of the mass within the aeroplane
always parallel to the aeroplane's vertical axis

qs.q: When an aeroplane is stationary on the ground, its total weight will act vertically
o: through a point defined as the datum point

qs.q: The weight of an aeroplane in level, non-accelerated flight is said to act
o: vertically through the centre of gravity
always along the vertical axis of the aeroplane

qs.q: The centre of gravity of an aeroplane
o: may only be moved if permitted by the regulating authority and endorsed in the C of A
must be maintained in a fixed position by careful distribution of the load
can be allowed to move between defined limits

qs.q: The centre of gravity is the
o: centre of thrust along the longitudinal axis, in relation to a datum line
neutral point along the longitudinal axis, in relation to a datum line
point where all the aircraft mass is considered to be concentrated

qs.q: The centre of gravity of a body is that point
o: where the sum of the external forces is equal to zero
which is always used as datum when computing moments
through which the sum of the forces of all masses of the body is considered to act

qs.q: An aeroplane is loaded with its centre of gravity towards the rear limit. This will result in:
o: a reduction in power required for a given speed
an increased risk of stalling due to a decrease in tailplane moment
a reduced fuel consumption as a result of reduced drag

qs.q: When the centre of gravity is at the forward limit, an aeroplane will be:
o: extremely stable and will require excessive elevator control to change pitch
extremely unstable and require excessive elevator control to change pitch
extremely stable and require small elevator control to change pitch

qs.q: What determines the longitudinal stability of an aeroplane?
o: The relationship of thrust and lift to weight and drag
The location of the centre of gravity with respect to the neutral point
The effectiveness of the horizontal stabiliser, rudder and rudder trim tab

qs.q: An aeroplane is said to be "neutrally stable". This is likely to:
o: cause the centre of gravity to move forwards
be caused by a centre of gravity which is towards the forward limit
be caused by a centre of gravity which is towards the rearward limit

qs.q: If the centre of gravity is near the forward limit the aeroplane will:
o: require elevator trim which will result in an increase in fuel consumption
benefit from reduced drag due to the decrease in angle of attack
require less power for a given airspeed

qs.q: During take-off you notice that, for a given elevator input, the aeroplane rotates much more rapidly than expected. This is an indication that:
o: the centre of pressure is aft of the centre of gravity
the centre of gravity may be towards the aft limit

qs.q: If the centre of gravity of an aeroplane moves forward during flight the elevator control will:
o: become heavier making the aeroplane more difficult to manoeuvre in pitch
become lighter making the aeroplane more difficult to manoeuvre in pitch
become heavier making the aeroplane more easy to manoeuvre in pitch

qs.q: The position of the centre of gravity can always be determined by:
o: subtracting the total moment from the total mass
dividing the total moment by the total mass
dividing the total mass by the total moment

qs.q: The stalling speed of an aeroplane will be highest when it is loaded with a:
o: high gross mass and aft centre of gravity
high gross mass and forward centre of gravity
low gross mass and aft centre of gravity
qs.ex: High mass and a forward CG (more tail download) give the highest stall speed.

qs.q: With the centre of gravity on the forward limit which of the following is to be expected?
o: A tendency to yaw to the right on take-off
A decrease of the stalling speed

qs.q: The Dry Operating Mass of an aeroplane includes:
o: Crew and crew baggage, catering, removable passenger service equipment, potable water and lavatory chemicals
Fuel and passengers' baggage and cargo

qs.q: At the flight preparation stage, the following parameters are available for determining the mass of the aircraft: (1) dry operating mass, (2) operating mass. Which statement is correct?
o: The dry operating mass includes fixed equipment needed to carry out a specific flight
The dry operating mass includes take-off fuel
The operating mass is the mass of the aeroplane without take-off fuel

qs.q: The term "Basic Empty Mass" includes the mass of the aeroplane structure complete with its power plants, systems, furnishings and other items of equipment considered an integral part of the configuration. Its value is
o: found in the latest version of the weighing schedule as corrected to allow for modifications
printed in the loading manual and includes unusable fuel
found in the flight manual and is inclusive of unusable fuel plus fluids contained in closed systems

qs.q: When establishing the mass breakdown of an aeroplane, the empty mass is defined as the sum of the:
o: basic mass plus special equipment mass
standard empty mass plus specific equipment mass plus trapped fluids plus unusable fuel mass
basic mass plus variable equipment mass

qs.q: An aeroplane is weighed: nose wheel 5330 kg, left main 12 370 kg, right main 12 480 kg. If the operational items amount to 1780 kg with a crew mass of 545 kg, the empty mass as entered in the weight schedule is:
qs.ex: The weight schedule records the mass as weighed: 5330 + 12 370 + 12 480 = 30 180 kg. Operational items (incl. crew) are added later to get the DOM.

qs.q: The take-off mass of an aeroplane is 117 000 kg, comprising a traffic load of 18 000 kg and fuel of 46 000 kg. What is the dry operating mass?
When preparing to weigh an aeroplane, which of the following is NOT required?
o: drain all chemical toilet fluid tanks

qs.q: An aeroplane may be weighed
o: at a specified "weighing location" on the airfield
in a quiet parking area clear of the normal manoeuvring area

qs.q: The mass of an aeroplane weighing more than 2000 kg must be determined prior to initial entry into service and thereafter
o: at intervals of 5 years if no modifications have taken place

qs.q: Where an operator uses an aircraft weighing less than 2000 kg, the re-weighing interval is
o: whenever a major repair/modification affecting weight and balance data is carried out
whenever the Certificate of Airworthiness is renewed

qs.q: An aeroplane is weighed prior to entry into service. Who is responsible for deriving the Dry Operating Mass from the weighed mass by adding the operational items?
The responsibility for determining the mass of operating items and crew included within the Dry Operating Mass lies with
o: the person compiling the weighing schedule

qs.q: A revenue flight; take-off mass not airfield limited. DOM 34 930 kg, performance-limited landing mass 55 000 kg, taxi fuel 350 kg, trip fuel 9730 kg, contingency and final reserve 1200 kg, alternate 1600 kg, 130 passengers at 84 kg with 14 kg baggage each, maximum traffic load. Determine the maximum cargo load without exceeding the limiting landing mass.

The empty mass of an aeroplane is 44 800 kg. Operational items (including crew standard mass of 1060 kg) are 2300 kg. If the maximum zero fuel mass is 65 500 kg, the maximum traffic load that could be carried is:

DOM 85 000 kg, performance-limited TOM 127 000 kg, performance-limited landing mass 98 500 kg, MZFM 89 800 kg; trip fuel 29 300 kg, contingency and final reserve 3600 kg, alternate 2800 kg. The maximum traffic load that can be carried is:

An additional baggage container is loaded into the aft cargo compartment but not entered in the load and trim sheet. The aeroplane will be heavier than expected and the calculated take-off safety speeds
o: are unaffected but will be increased

qs.q: Fuel loaded is 15 400 kg but is entered in the load and trim sheet as 14 500 kg. The error is not detected, but the crew will notice that
o: speed at unstick will be higher than expected
V1 will be reached sooner than expected
the aeroplane will rotate much earlier than expected

qs.q: When considering the effects of increased mass on an aeroplane, which is true?
o: Gradient of climb for a given power setting will be higher

qs.q: An aeroplane is loaded with 16 500 litres of fuel at a density of 780 kg/m³. This is entered into the load sheet as 16 500 kg. As a result the aeroplane is
o: lighter than anticipated and the calculated safety speeds will be too high
heavier than anticipated and the calculated safety speeds will be too high
lighter than anticipated and the calculated safety speeds will be too low
qs.ex: 16 500 L × 0.78 = 12 870 kg, so the aircraft is lighter than the sheet says and the computed speeds are too high.

qs.q: A flight benefits from an unforecast strong tailwind. On arrival a straight-in approach and immediate landing clearance are given. The landing mass will be higher than planned and
o: the approach path will be steeper
the landing distance required will be longer
the approach path will be steeper and threshold speed higher

qs.q: Determine the landing mass for this single-engine aeroplane: standard empty mass 1764 lb, optional equipment 35 lb, pilot + front passenger 300 lb, cargo 350 lb, ramp (block) fuel 60 gal, trip fuel 35 gal, fuel density 6 lb/gal.
qs.ex: Zero-fuel mass 2449 lb + block fuel 360 lb − trip 210 lb = 2599 lb.

qs.q: MSTOM 48 000 kg, MSLM 44 000 kg, MZFM 36 000 kg; taxi fuel 600 kg, contingency 900 kg, alternate 800 kg, final reserve 1100 kg, trip fuel 9000 kg. Determine the actual take-off mass:
qs.ex: MZFM + take-off fuel (9000 + 900 + 800 + 1100) = 47 800 kg is the limit.

qs.q: If an aeroplane is at a higher mass than anticipated, for a given airspeed the angle of attack will
o: remain constant, drag will decrease and endurance will decrease
remain constant, drag will increase and endurance will increase
be greater, drag will increase and endurance will decrease

qs.q: DOM 90 000 kg, block fuel 30 000 kg, taxi fuel 800 kg, maximum take-off mass 145 000 kg. The traffic load available is:
DOM 2000 kg; maximum take-off, landing and zero-fuel masses all 3500 kg; block fuel 550 kg, taxi fuel 50 kg. The available payload is:
The maximum fuel that can be loaded is 3800 US gallons. With a specific gravity of 0.79, the mass of fuel which may be loaded is
DOM 38 000 kg, MSTOM 72 000 kg, MLM 65 000 kg, MZFM 61 000 kg, fuel burn 8000 kg, take-off fuel 10 300 kg. The maximum allowed take-off mass and payload are respectively:

Structural limits: maximum ramp 69 900 kg, MTOM 69 300 kg, MLM 58 900 kg, MZFM 52 740 kg. Performance-limited TOM 67 450 kg, performance-limited LM 55 470 kg. DOM 34 900 kg, trip fuel 6200 kg, taxi 250 kg, contingency & final reserve 1300 kg, alternate 1100 kg. The maximum traffic load is:

Performance-limited TOM 93 500 kg, expected landing mass at destination 81 700 kg, maximum certificated landing mass 86 300 kg, fuel on board 16 500 kg. A diversion is made to an en-route alternate (not performance-limited for landing); fuel remaining at landing 10 300 kg. The landing mass:
o: is 87 300 kg and excess structural stress could result
is 83 200 kg, in excess of the regulated landing mass, and could result in overrunning the runway
must be reduced to 81 700 kg to avoid a high-speed approach

qs.q: Take-off mass 302 550 kg; fuel on board at take-off (including contingency and alternate of 19 450 kg) 121 450 kg; DOM 161 450 kg. The useful load will be:

Total mass 7500 kg, CG at station 80.5, aft CG limit station 79.5. How much cargo must be shifted from the aft compartment (station 150) to the forward compartment (station 30) to move the CG to the aft limit?
The weighing schedule gives empty mass 57 320 kg, nominal DOM 60 120 kg and MZFM 72 100 kg. Which statement is correct?
o: operational items 2800 kg and maximum useful load 14 780 kg
operational items 2800 kg and maximum traffic load 11 980 kg
operational items 2800 kg and maximum traffic load 14 780 kg

qs.q: Block fuel 40 000 kg, trip fuel 29 000 kg, taxi fuel 800 kg; MTOM 170 000 kg, MLM 148 500 kg, MZFM 112 500 kg, DOM 80 400 kg. The maximum traffic load is:
The Zero Fuel Mass and the Dry Operating Mass:
o: differ by the mass of usable fuel
differ by the value of the traffic load mass

qs.q: Certified MTOM 141 500 kg, performance-limited TOM 137 300 kg, DOM 58 400 kg excluding crew and crew hand baggage of 640 kg, crew baggage in hold 110 kg, fuel on board 60 700 kg. Calculate the useful load.
The term 'Basic Empty Mass' includes the mass of the aeroplane structure with its powerplants, systems, furnishings and integral equipment. Its value is
o: printed in the loading manual and includes unusable fuel
found in the latest version of the weighing schedule as corrected to allow for modifications
inclusive of an allowance for crew, crew baggage and other operating items; it is entered in the loading manifest

qs.q: Basic empty mass 3000 kg; maximum take-off, landing and zero-fuel masses all 5200 kg; ramp fuel 650 kg, taxi fuel 50 kg. The payload available is:
qs.ex: Take-off fuel 600; 5200 − 3000 − 600 = 1600 kg (taking basic empty mass as the DOM).

qs.q: The Dry Operating Mass is the total mass of the aeroplane ready for a specific type of operation but excluding:
On an aeroplane without a central fuel tank, the maximum Zero Fuel Mass is related to:
o: the bending moment at the wing root

qs.q: M to N 750 NM, no fuel at N. TAS 380 kt, 30 kt headwind M→N, fuel flow 5700 kg/h, reserve 500 kg (unused), mass less fuel and traffic load 52 000 kg, MTOM at M 91 000 kg, at N 88 000 kg, MLM at N 77 500 kg, at M 75 000 kg. Find (i) maximum traffic load M→N, (ii) maximum traffic load N→M.

PLTOM 45 000 lb, PLLM 40 000 lb, flight fuel 4000 lb, reserve 800 lb, DOM 25 000 lb. Find (i) the traffic load, (ii) whether additional reserve fuel can be carried without affecting the traffic load, and how much.

P to Q (no fuel at Q) and back. Max traffic load off-loaded at Q and uplifted from Q. Distance 610 NM; mass without fuel and traffic load 36 500 kg; MLM 52 400 kg; MTOM 63 000 kg; reserve (unused) 4000 kg; additional fuel per flight 500 kg; consumption 1350 kg/h; GS P→Q 240 kt, Q→P 280 kt. Find (i) fuel to lift at P, (ii) max traffic load P→Q, (iii) max traffic load Q→P.
MSTOM 80 000 lb, MSLM 64 500 lb, DOM 50 000 lb, flight fuel 6000 (book: kg), reserve 1500. Find the traffic load that can be carried.

A to B: max take-off mass (structural) 82 000 lb, mass without fuel and traffic load 50 000 lb, PLLM 64 000 lb, fuel for A→B 16 000 lb, reserve 8000 lb. If the aircraft lands at B having used 500 lb of reserve, what maximum traffic load can be carried?

A to B: max permissible TOM 82 000 lb, mass without fuel and traffic load 50 000 lb, max permissible landing mass 69 000 lb, fuel A→B 16 000 lb, reserve 3000 lb. (i) Maximum traffic load? (ii) Can additional reserve fuel be carried without affecting it?

M to N and back with max traffic load each way, no fuel at N: 80 NM; GS M→N 70 kt, N→M 110 kt; 410 kg/h; MTOM at M 6180 kg, MLM at N 5740 kg, MTOM at N 5800 kg, MLM at M 5460 kg, MZFM 5180 kg, mass less fuel and traffic load 4400 kg, reserve 250 kg (unused). Find (i) max traffic load M→N, (ii) N→M.
Max T/O mass 51.0 t, RTOM 50.0 t, max landing mass 44.2 t, RLM 43.2 t, MZFM 45.1 t, APS mass 27.5 t, trip fuel 4.2 t, reserve 1.0 t. Find the traffic load that can be carried.

Max take-off mass 80 000 lb, max landing mass 60 000 lb, DOM 48 000 lb, TAS 200 kt, track 350°, W/V 350/20, distance 1350 NM, fuel consumption 2500 lb/h, reserve 3500 lb. Find the traffic load that can be carried.

MSTOM 55 000 kg, MSLM 52 000 kg, MZFM 38 000 kg, DOM 29 000 kg, consumption 1600 kg/h, distance 1500 NM, reserve 2750 kg, TAS 260 kt. Winds: 20 kt headwind to half way, then 60 kt tailwind. (i) Max traffic load in still air; (ii) with the winds.
Find the maximum traffic load: flying time 3 h 30 min, FC 1500 kg/h, reserve fuel 45 min, restricted take-off mass 45 000 kg, DOM 37 525 kg.
MSTOM 82 000 lb, MSLM 64 500 lb, DOM 50 000 lb, flight fuel 16 000 lb, reserve 1500 lb. Calculate the payload if the aircraft is to use 700 lb of reserve fuel after reaching destination.
In a neutrally stable aircraft the centre of gravity is located:
o: at or very near the aerodynamic centre
too far aft of the aerodynamic centre
too far forward of the aerodynamic centre
qs.ex: Neutral stability: CG at or very near the aerodynamic centre (neutral point).

qs.q: Structural integrity of the wing root will be adversely affected by:
o: increasing the number of fasteners at the wing root
exceeding maximum authorised mass including fuel

qs.q: Calculate the total fuel required for a turbojet: thrust 80 kN, SFC 0.6 kg/(s·kN), flight time 30 min.
